name: Lyrical Ballads and the Lake Poets
description: The poetry produced by Wordsworth, Coleridge and Southey in and after Lyrical Ballads (1798): a verse of humble life, of meditative blank verse, and of the mind's intercourse with natural place, together with the criticism that justified it.
historical_context: Shaped by the enthusiasm and then the disappointment produced by the French Revolution, by the withdrawal into the countryside at Racedown, Alfoxton and Grasmere, by the publishing boom of the 1790s, and by the war and domestic repressions of 1792-1815. Wordsworth's Lakeland residence, Coleridge's journalism and lecturing, and the three poets' shared ambition to a national poetry out of the failure of their Bristol and Oxford schemes of the 1790s gave the movement its institutions and its quarrels.
aesthetic_principles: Poetry as the spontaneous overflow of powerful feeling, taking its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity; the real language of men and a deliberate lowering of poetic diction; the poet as a man speaking to men; humble and rustic life as a school of permanent feeling; the balance of the ordinary with the imaginative; the ballad, the lyric and the long meditative blank-verse poem as the principal forms.
defining_characteristics: The conversation poem (Wordsworth's 'Lines written a few miles above Tintern Abbey', The Excursion; Coleridge's 'This Lime-Tree Bower My Prison', 'Frost at Midnight', 'Dejection: An Ode'); the lyrical ballad and the poem of humble narrative; the supernatural ballad treated realistically in its psychology; the sonnet of political and personal occasion; blank-verse topographical meditation; the autobiographical poem of growth; the preface and supplementary essay as parts of the poetic work.
historical_significance: It is the founding movement of English Romanticism and of the modern idea of the poet as a maker whose sensibility and memory are themselves the subject of the work. The Preface of 1802 to Lyrical Ballads and Coleridge's Biographia Literaria remain the two central documents of English criticism about poetry, and the verse of the movement set the terms on which later nineteenth-century poetry, British and American, was written and judged.

name: Blake and the Illuminated Prophecy
description: William Blake's practice of engraving poem and design together, and the body of short lyric and long prophetic verse that his method produced.
historical_context: Blake worked in London as an engraver trained in the workshop method of James Basire and formed in circles of religious dissent and radical politics that admired Priestley and Paine. The depression of print after the war with France, the failure of his exhibition of 1809, and the patronage of Thomas Butts and later of John Linnell determined the small circulations of his books. His visionary politics answer the American and French Revolutions, Methodism, and the mechanical philosophy associated with Newton and Locke.
aesthetic_principles: Imagination as the divine humanity and the only faculty of knowledge; the refusal of any division between sense and spirit; contrariety as the condition of progress; hostility to moral law experienced as repression and to a single vision confined to measurement; the illuminated page as a unity of text and figure; the aphorism, the song and the prophetic book as complementary vehicles.
defining_characteristics: The emblem book and the song cycle, with its paired states of innocence and experience and its repetitions; the long prophetic book with its personal mythology of Urizen, Los, Enitharmon and Orc; the brief lyric and the epigram; the polemic marginalia; the combination of relief etching, lettering and illumination.
historical_significance: Blake made the theory and the practice of imaginative art a single thing, and anticipated the modern sense of the artist's book and of visual poetry. His lyrics of innocence and experience are among the most widely read short poems in English, and the prophetic books expanded what the Romantic long poem could contain.

name: Byron and the Byronic Revolt
description: Byron's poetry and prose, and the fashion for the defiant, guilty, solitary hero that they created, in narrative poem, satire, verse drama and letter.
historical_context: Childe Harold's Pilgrimage (1812) appeared amid the Peninsular War and made its author famous in a season. The separation of 1816 and the social ostracism that followed gave the revolted hero its biographical authority; the Italian years from 1816, the friendship with Shelley, the circles at Venice and Pisa, and the intervention in the Greek cause, with his death at Missolonghi in 1824, completed the public career. The closing of the London stage to his drama pushed his later plays into closet form.
aesthetic_principles: The dignity of the defiant individual; pride, guilt and endurance as the proper matter of poem; a deliberate mixture of the elevated and the familiar; sincerity as performance and the ironised autobiographical persona; scepticism about systems and about the perfectibility of institutions; the Spenserian stanza and ottava rima as the vehicles of the narrative and the satirical poem.
defining_characteristics: The Byronic hero, superior, transgressive, self-punishing and at war with heaven and society; the pilgrimage and traveller's poem; the Oriental tale with its erotic and cruel setting; the satirical romance in ottava rima with its intrusive narrator; the dramatised monologue of Cain, Manfred and Sardanapalus; the autobiographical prose of the letters and the journal.
historical_significance: Byron made European fame and literary notoriety a single fact, and set the pattern of the self-mythologising artist that the nineteenth century universalised. Don Juan carried Augustan satire into a new freedom of narrative manner, and the Eastern tales and the monologues of revolt shaped popular romantic drama and the lyric of defiance for a century and more.

name: Shelley and Radical Romanticism
description: The poetry and prose of Percy Bysshe Shelley, and the circle of writers who joined a programme of political, religious and domestic emancipation to a theory of poetry as the highest form of moral knowledge.
historical_context: Shelley's expulsion from Oxford in 1811 for a pamphlet on the necessity of atheism, his elopement with Harriet Westbrook in the same year, his attachment to Mary Godwin from 1814 and their Swiss summer of 1816, which produced Frankenstein, the Italian exile from 1818, and the small private printings circulated among a few friends gave radical Romanticism its shape. Its occasion was the failure of reform after Waterloo, the Peterloo massacre of 1819 with the Six Acts that followed, and the revival of Italian revolutionary expectation at Naples and Pisa.
aesthetic_principles: Poetry as the record of the best and happiest moments of the happiest and best minds; the imagination as the great instrument of moral good; the conviction that governments, religions and the relations of the sexes are opinions and can be remade; the sublime understood as an intellectual as well as a natural effect; a deliberate difficulty of allegory in the lyric and the closet drama.
defining_characteristics: The political song, address and broadsheet; the Platonizing hymn to intellectual beauty and to the powers of night and wind; the great lyric meditation in Spenserian or mixed stanza; the Promethean closet drama with its chorus and its cosmic argument; the essay as criticism and manifesto; the elegy and the epitaph.
historical_significance: Shelley stated most exactly the Romantic identification of imagination with liberty, and his criticism, with Coleridge's, formed the theory of poetry that the nineteenth century inherited. His political lyrics were taken up by later radical and labour traditions, and Prometheus Unbound and Adonais set the standard for the philosophical drama and for the modern elegy.

name: Keats and the Sensuous Ode
description: The short and intense career of John Keats, in which the elaborate Elizabethanizing lyric, the sonnet of rivalry and mortality, and the odes of 1819 turned sensation and patience into a poetic theory.
historical_context: Keats came to print out of the Hunt circle and the journals associated with Leigh Hunt, whose worship of Spenser, Shakespeare and the Elizabethans set its face against the classicism of the Reviews. The deaths of his mother and his brother, his own illness, the strain of the touring of 1818, and the hostility of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine and the Quarterly Review determined the brevity of the career; the Rome winter and his death there in February 1821 closed it.
aesthetic_principles: Negative capability, the ability to remain in uncertainties and doubts without reaching after fact and reason; the apprehension of beauty as the test of truth; the primacy of sensuous particular over abstract statement; the assumption that a poet has no identity and lives in its creations; a deliberate sonorous and archaic diction; the ode as the form of a mind thinking in its own pleasures.
defining_characteristics: The elaborate Spenserianizing romance-lyric and the ballad of enchantment; the odes of 1819 in ten-line lyric stanza and the fourteen-line Induction; the sonnet of address, rivalry and mortality; the verse epistle in couplets and blank verse; the allegorical romance in verse; the letter as criticism.
historical_significance: Keats made the lyric ode a modern form of thought about transience and art, and supplied the vocabulary by which later aestheticism and much modern criticism have described the poet's relation to belief. The odes, Lamia and the Hyperion fragments remain central examples of the English high lyric.

name: Scott, the Ballad Revival and the Historical Novel
description: Walter Scott's editing and imitation of border and national ballad, his metrical tales and romances in verse, and the Waverley novels that made the historical fiction of an entire people a major form, together with the ballad collections and antiquarian enterprises that attended them.
historical_context: The Minstrelsy of the Scottish Border (1802-03) grew out of Scott's antiquarian collecting with John Leyden and James Hogg; the metrical tales of 1805-1815 answered the success of Byron; the Waverley novels appeared from 1814 anonymously or under the designation of the 'Author of Waverley', at a moment of English curiosity about the Highland and border past after the '45 and the mass recruiting of the war years. The failure of the Ballantyne printing firm in 1826, which ruined Scott publicly, forced the later novels and the journal of the last years into the expanding market of serial and annual print.
aesthetic_principles: History as manners, costume and speech rather than as argument; the ballad as the authentic voice of a nation and an age; the mixed vernacular and the dialect of the humble narrator; the romance plot set against documented social change; a conservative sympathy with the losing side and with the vanishing past.
defining_characteristics: The edited ballad collection with its prefatory essays, imitations and doubtful attestations; the metrical tale and romance in verse; the Tales of My Landlord frame and its editorial persona; the historical novel of a frontier or transitional period (Waverley, Guy Mannering, The Antiquary, Old Mortality, The Heart of Midlothian, Rob Roy, The Bride of Lammermoor, Ivanhoe, Kenilworth, The Monastery and The Abbot); the romance of the Covenanting and Jacobite risings.
historical_significance: Scott invented the modern historical novel and set the model of national-popular ballad scholarship. The collections and their essays were the chief engine of the Romantic taste for the popular and the primitive, and the novels were imitated across the century by Dickens, Thackeray, Manzoni, Hugo and Cooper.

name: Austen and the Novel of Manners
description: The published novels of Jane Austen and the related comedy of provincial and genteel life, in which judgement, self-knowledge and the ethics of the marriage market are conducted through irony, dialogue and the restricted point of view of an intelligent but limited observer.
historical_context: Austen wrote in the gentry households of Steventon, Southampton, Bath and Chawton between the 1790s and 1816, in a decade of war, of the disposal of livings, and of the anxieties of rank and income. Sense and Sensibility was her first publication, in 1811; Northanger Abbey and Persuasion appeared together after her death in 1818. The three-volume novel, the circulating library and anonymous publication under the designation 'By the Author of...' defined the market in which she worked.
aesthetic_principles: The observation of three or four families in a country village as the proper canvas, in her own account of her work; the primacy of judgement over sensibility and of self-examination over admiration; a morality of constancy, gratitude and duty inside the marriage plot; free indirect discourse as the means of showing error and its correction; a defended and ironic use of the romance and Gothic conventions she employs.
defining_characteristics: The comedy of misunderstanding and corrected self-knowledge (Pride and Prejudice, Emma); the heroine's education in sensibility and prudence; the marriage plot as an economy of rank and fortune; the genteel parable of influence and dependency; anti-Gothic comedy (Northanger Abbey); conversation and letter as the vehicles of moral discovery.
historical_significance: Austen perfected the novel of social judgement in a small compass and made free indirect discourse a standard technique of modern prose fiction. Her work is the point from which the nineteenth-century realistic novel of manners descends, and it has been central both to the history of the novel as a literary art and to the later criticism of women's writing.

name: Philosophical Fiction and the Godwin Circle
description: The fiction and political philosophy of William Godwin, Mary Wollstonecraft and Mary Shelley, and the related tale of idea, in which institutions, education, property and the relations of the sexes are tested by argument and narrative experiment.
historical_context: Godwin's Enquiry Concerning Political Justice (1793) and his novels of the 1790s supplied the speculative frame; Wollstonecraft's first Vindication (1792), her later fiction, and Godwin's Memoirs of its author (1798) made the case of women part of the same argument; Godwin's second marriage in 1801, his failure as a juvenile bookseller, and his daughter Mary's Frankenstein (1818) and The Last Man (1826) carry the circle into the 1820s, in a climate of post-Waterloo repression and of anxiety about scientific and social change.
aesthetic_principles: Institutions as the result of opinion, and opinion as changeable by reason; the novel as a proper vehicle of moral and political inquiry; the interest of a tale lying in mind, motive and consequence rather than in incident; benevolence and private judgement against public authority; the education of feeling as the end of narrative; a later and sceptical revision of the doctrine of perfectibility.
defining_characteristics: The analytic novel of pursuit and disclosure (Caleb Williams); the domestic and philosophical tale of the woman without protection; the tale of scientific transgression and its consequences (Frankenstein); the post-apocalyptic plague romance (The Last Man); the essay-tale and the juvenile library with its moral apparatus; anonymous or initialled publication of radical work.
historical_significance: The circle joined the Enlightenment argument about institutions to Romantic narrative and produced the founding works both of the political novel of inquiry and of scientific romance. Frankenstein created a myth still used to think about making, responsibility and technology, and Wollstonecraft's and Godwin's writings formed the case for women's education that later feminist thought developed.

name: The Regency Stage and Popular Drama
description: London theatre between the patent controversies and the Reform era: melodrama, nautical and sentimental drama, comic opera and burletta, the restoration of Shakespeare from eighteenth-century alteration, and the actor-management; with the drama written by the Romantic poets for the theatre and for the closet.
historical_context: The patent system confined serious drama to the two patent houses and the Haymarket until the theatre reforms of the 1840s, so the popular stage developed in the minor theatres as melodrama, burletta, pantomime and spectacle. The Old Price riot of 1809 marked the audience's own politics against Covent Garden's management; the long direction of Drury Lane by John Philip Kemble, the sudden stardom of Edmund Kean from 1814, William Macready's reforming acting and management, and the tragedy of Charles Mayne Young set the taste of the period.
aesthetic_principles: Spectacle, moral clarity and the pathos of the virtuous poor and the persecuted heroine in melodrama; the defence of 'legitimate' drama on grounds of national literature and taste; a movement from altered and adapted Shakespeare toward the earlier texts; and a verse drama written by poets largely indifferent to, or excluded by, the manager.
defining_characteristics: Melodrama and the nautical and military drama of the war and peace; burletta and comic opera; domestic and sentimental tragedy; the closet tragedy of Manfred, The Cenci, Prometheus Unbound and Count Julian; Shakespeare editing and revival; the prologue and the theatrical occasional verse; the playbill and the theatrical corner of the annual and the magazine.
historical_significance: It is the theatre in which the modern ideas of the manager's or director's responsibility and of the literary text's authority began, and melodrama became the deepest popular form of moral narrative of the nineteenth century. Because the licensed stage would not take the poets' tragedy, the Romantic closet drama became a major form of reading drama in English.

name: Romantic Essay, Criticism and the Review
description: The prose of the great quarterly and monthly reviews and of the essayists who wrote for and beside them: Hazlitt's characters and table-talk, Lamb's Elia, De Quincey's literary confessions, Jeffrey, Lockhart and Wilson, and the periodical culture that made criticism a profession.
historical_context: The Edinburgh Review from 1802, the Quarterly Review from 1809, Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine from 1817 and the Westminster Review from 1824, with the literary annual and the keepsake from the early 1820s, made the review the central institution of literary judgement. A Regency reading public, the growing circulations of London and the provinces, a more secure copyright after the decisions of the 1770s and 1780s, and the personal rivalries of Wordsworth, Byron and Scott gave the criticism its polemical energy.
aesthetic_principles: Character writing as the analysis of a mind; sympathy and imagination as the critic's instruments; the familiar essay's mixture of memory, humour and book-love; the literary confession, in which the dream becomes a structure of prose; periodical attack as a public moral act; and the theory of poetry's value stated in lecture, preface and review.
defining_characteristics: The review article and the pamphlet; the book of characters and the lecture series; the familiar essay under a pseudonymous self; autobiographical confessional prose; the annual's miscellany of prose and verse; the magazine's tale, sketch and criticism.
historical_significance: These writers established modern criticism as a profession and the essay as a major literary form, and their quarrels defined the idea of Romantic literature before the word was current. Hazlitt's and Coleridge's lectures remain the most quoted account of Elizabethan and contemporary literature in English, and Lamb's and De Quincey's prose is the source of the modern essay of memory and self-analysis.

name: Regency Popular Verse and the Annual Public
description: The widely read verse of the Regency and late-Romantic publishing world that grew up beside the Lake poets and the younger generation: Samuel Rogers's polished verse essays, Thomas Campbell's national and revolutionary lyrics, Thomas Moore's Irish and Oriental romances and satires, and the women poets of the periodicals and gift books, Felicia Hemans and Letitia Elizabeth Landon.
historical_context: Made possible by the expansion of the literary periodical after 1802, by the rise of the annual and keepsake from The Forget-Me-Not (1823) and The Keepsake (1828) onward, and by a reading public that had grown with the war and the post-war book trade. Rogers published slowly and by subscription among Whig patrons; Campbell rose with The Pleasures of Hope (1799) and lived on the radical causes of Poland and the American west; Moore was famous and notorious at once; Hemans and Landon were made by the Literary Gazette (1824) and the annuals, and were read, imitated and reviewed on a scale the Lake poets never reached.
aesthetic_principles: Polished and public verse: the closed and epigrammatic line, the memorable refrain, and a deliberate difficulty-free smoothness; sentiment realised through situation rather than argument; the topical and occasional poem as a legitimate form; national song and the ballad of historic grievance treated as serious lyric; an ethics of domestic and feminine feeling, and its conscious rhetorical construction.
defining_characteristics: the verse essay and the epistolary poem of place; the lyric of national memory and protest; Oriental and romantic narrative verse in the Aftermath of Byron; the annual and keepsake poem with its engraved illustration; the ballad of domestic tragedy and historic anecdote; a close dependence on the review and the literary gazette; verse written for a gift-book market and for monthly periodicals
historical_significance: The best-sellers of their day, these poets set the terms on which Romantic verse reached a mass reading public, and they carried the Romantic inheritance into the Victorian annual, the cathedral praxis of Hemans's hymns, and the poetry of women's experience. Their later dismissal as 'secondary' Romanticism is itself a critical history worth recording: Landon was called the female Byron by Jerdan, and Hemans was set aside by precisely the Victorian generation she helped to form.

name: Labouring-Class and Village Poetry
description: Verse written by and about those who worked the land and the handicraft trades, and published into a literary system that was organised around leisure and patronage. Robert Bloomfield's rural narrative of husbandry, Ebeneezer Pinder's self-published labouring miscellany, John Clare's enclosed Helpston and its bird-life, and the lesser patterers and mechanic poets of the 1810s and 1820s make up the current body of records.
historical_context: It flourished in the decades of wartime and post-war dearth, when enclosure remade the countryside, when the price of bread and the depression of 1815-1821 hit agricultural labour hardest, and when a subsistence and subscription publishing economy made it possible for a ploughman or a boot-maker to be printed at all. Bloomfield was encouraged by the Bowood connection and by Ackermann's engraving programme; Pinder subscribed his first volume together with two other labouring writers; Clare was launched by bookseller-publisher John Taylor and protected by patron subscribers who bought his copyright. The poets are the inheritors of Robert Burns and of the earlier eighteenth-century 'farming poets', and were read beside the Lake poets whom they resembled and differed from.
aesthetic_principles: Village and field as sufficient subject; a topographical fidelity to a single parish and its seasons; the plain and unornamented diction that the poets themselves defended against classical allusion; the observation of birds, weather and hedgerow as a serious poetic occupation; the autobiographical frame of difficulty and the claim to authorship by experience rather than by education; and an occasional, sometimes rueful, self-consciousness about the reviewing press.
defining_characteristics: Rural labour, husbandry and the parish as the primary subject matter; Plain diction and deliberate avoidance of classical learning; Natural history observation as an organizing poetic mode; Enclosure, agrarian change and rural poverty as explicit themes; Publication by subscription, by provincial press or by a single sympathetic London bookseller; Patronage, copyright purchase and the 'protected' poet as a recurring biographical fact; Debts to Robert Burns and to the earlier eighteenth-century farming poets; Concentration in one locality, especially Helpston and the Soham country
historical_significance: It carried the Romantic attention to ordinary speech and rural life into the sphere of class, and it exposed the literary marketplace's treatment of writers who could not control their own copyrights or their own reputations. Clare in particular, long dismissed as a naïve natural poet, is now read as a major and formally experimental writer of enclosure and mental crisis, and his case forced nineteenth-century arguments about patronage, lunacy law and the ownership of a poet's papers that continue to shape editorial practice.
